question: On 12 July 2026, Spiegel Online1 ran a piece on large-scale bot networks active mainly on X and Instagram. With Russian-based actors pulling the strings, the bots are programmed to spread disinformation about German politicians, taking aim at all democratic parties, with the exception of politicians from the AfD and the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance. According to media reports2, what we are witnessing is a continuation of the Russian-led ‘Matryoshka’ campaign which, records show, began in 2023 at the latest. 1.

Against this background and in view of the upcoming state elections in Germany, not to mention the elections coming up in various EU Member States in 2027, is the Commission checking whether the very large online platforms (VLOPs) concerned are operating in accordance with the Digital Services Act (DSA) and taking down unlawful content bearing counterfeit media logos in a timely manner?

What specific action has the Commission taken against the VLOPs to date in order to effectively disable coordinated bot networks that pose a systemic threat to public discourse and elections, pursuant to Article 34 DSA?
What has it done to verify compliance with, and enforce, the bot network guidance in its DSA elections toolkit, and is it considering introducing any further enforcement measures?

Der Spiegel, „Wladimir Putin: So wirbt der russische Präsident für AfD und BSW“ [‘Vladimir Putin: how the Russian President is throwing his weight behind AfD and BSW’], 2026. https://www.spiegel.de/wissenschaft/mensch/wladimir-putin-so-wirbt-der-russische-praesident-fuer-afd-undbsw-kolumne-a-60288130-2d29-4dd2-b3b6-5ac10cb62fdd.

2 FAZ, „Prorussisches Bot-Netz greift in Landtagswahl ein“ [‘Pro-Russian bot network meddles in state parliament elections’], 2026. https://www.faz.net/aktuell/politik/ausland/prorussisches-bot-netz-greift-inlandtagswahlkampf-ein-200994855.html. 1
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (14.9.2026) The Commission is closely monitoring reports concerning coordinated inauthentic behaviour and foreign interference. Under the Digital Services Act (DSA)1, very large online platforms (VLOPs) must identify, assess and mitigate systemic risks linked to their services, including risks to electoral processes, civic discourse, and inauthentic or automated use.
They must also act diligently against illegal content, including counterfeit material infringing intellectual property, when aware of it, and are subject to annual independent audits.

The Commission is supervising whether VLOPs such as X and Meta comply with these obligations, including on notice-and-action mechanisms, transparency reporting, data access and mitigation of risks linked to deceptive use of media identities and logos where this may breach EU or national law.
The Commission uses the full range of DSA tools, including requests for information, scrutiny of risk assessments and mitigation measures, and investigations where appropriate.

Formal proceedings have been opened against X2 and Meta3 in areas relevant to electoral integrity and civic discourse: X concerning information manipulation on the platform, and Meta concerning deceptive advertisements and coordinated inauthentic behaviour in the EU4. The Commission also monitors the implementation of the 2025 DSA Elections Guidelines5.

Together with the Code of Conduct on Disinformation6 and its voluntary Rapid Response System7, this supports election preparedness and cooperation. As announced in the Democracy Shield8, the Commission, with national Digital Services Coordinators and the European Cooperation Network on Elections, will update the DSA Elections Toolkit9 and develop an incident and crisis protocol under the DSA.
